title: The Early Creed of 1 Corinthians 15

keyTerms.d: Paul says he “delivered” (Greek paredōka) what he “received” (parelabon) — the precise idiom used in Judaism for the transmission of authoritative tradition, the equivalent of the rabbinic masar and qibbel. Paul is not narrating his own experience here; he is handing on something handed to him.

That 1 Corinthians 15:3-5 (with the list extending through verse 7) is a pre-Pauline creed is broadly recognized in the scholarship: a summary of the gospel that the earliest believers were already confessing before Paul ever picked up a pen. Paul then adds his own experience, “last of all” (15:8), closing the list rather than typifying it.

The phrase “for our sins,” the verb “he has been raised” in a particular perfect form, the expression “the twelve,” and “according to the Scriptures” cluster non-Pauline vocabulary into a few lines. The Aramaic name Kēphas points to a Semitic-speaking milieu rather than proving non-Pauline wording, since Paul himself usually calls him Cephas.

The lines fall into balanced clauses, each introduced by the Greek hoti (“that”), in a fourfold rhythm — died, was buried, was raised, appeared — that reads as a confession to be memorized rather than prose to be composed on the fly.

Paul says that “after three years” he went up to Jerusalem “to get acquainted with” Cephas, staying fifteen days, and that he also saw James the Lord’s brother (Galatians 1:18-19). The verb occurs only here in the New Testament and connotes inquiry — getting to know a person and, plausibly, his account.

The firmest external anchor for Pauline chronology is the Gallio inscription from Delphi, which fixes Gallio’s proconsulship of Achaia to about AD 51-52; via Acts 18:12 it anchors Paul’s stay in Corinth, and the earlier stages of his career are reckoned backward from that fixed point. It dates Gallio, and so anchors Paul; it does not by itself date the creed.

“The Twelve” is not a running head-count; it is the fixed name of the apostolic body, and the New Testament uses it that way even where it cannot mean twelve people — a deliberate institutional label, not a slip of the tally.

The tight, rhythmic core — died, buried, raised, “appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve” (vv. 3b-5) — reads as a single fixed unit. A composite text with an early core is still an early core — and the early core is all the argument needs.

derive.q: Paul introduces the lines with “I delivered to you … what I also received” — so the passage is…?
derive.ans: handed-on tradition, not his own composition
derive.why: Paul uses the technical language of rabbinic tradition — receiving and delivering a fixed body of teaching. He is not narrating his own experience here; he is handing on something handed to him, a formula older than the letter that contains it.

derive.q: The Aramaic-original claim is contested — so the pre-Pauline case rests on…?
derive.ans: the cumulative weight, not the Aramaic question
derive.why: Some scholars, including those who fully accept the formula’s antiquity, think it was composed in Greek among Greek-speaking Jewish Christians. The pre-Pauline character of the formula does not stand or fall on the Aramaic question; it rests on the cumulative weight of the receiving/delivering language, the non-Pauline diction, and the creedal structure.

derive.q: Paul meets Cephas and James three years after his conversion, and the tradition must predate his receipt of it — so its origin falls…?
derive.ans: within roughly two to five years of the crucifixion
derive.why: Most historians place the crucifixion around AD 30-33 and Paul’s conversion within a year or three of it. Whether Paul first received the formula at his conversion or had it confirmed in that face-to-face fortnight in Jerusalem, the tradition itself must predate his receipt of it. That pushes its origin into the first half of the 30s — within roughly two to five years of the crucifixion, and arguably less.

derive.q: An inscription fixes a Roman proconsul’s term to about AD 51-52 — so it…?
derive.ans: anchors Paul’s chronology, not the creed itself
derive.why: Because Acts 18:12 has Paul brought before Gallio’s tribunal at Corinth, the inscription dates Gallio and thereby anchors Paul’s stay in Corinth; the earlier stages of his career are reckoned backward from that fixed point. It dates Gallio, and so anchors Paul; it does not by itself date the creed.

derive.q: The four-part claim was recited within a few years of the cross by the very people named as its witnesses — so the theory that it grew by accretion over decades…?
derive.ans: is foreclosed: the window is too narrow
derive.why: The four-part claim — Christ died, was buried, was raised, and appeared — was not a late development but the bedrock confession of the movement from its earliest traceable moment, recited by the very people (Peter, James, “the twelve”) who claimed to be its witnesses. The window is too narrow for legendary embellishment to have done its slow work, and the named, living witnesses functioned as a check.

derive.q: Grant all of it: the belief is early and sincere. Does the creed, by itself, prove the resurrection?
derive.ans: no — that is a further inference, argued on separate grounds
derive.why: That the first disciples were convinced they had seen the risen Jesus — and convinced very soon — is a historical datum the evidence supports strongly. That their conviction was true is a further inference, argued on separate grounds (the inadequacy of alternative explanations, the empty tomb, the transformation of the disciples, the conversion of skeptics like James and Paul). The creed is the indispensable first premise of the resurrection case, not the whole of it.

honestState.p1: The early date of the creed is about as close to a consensus as ancient history offers. What is not seriously disputed is the narrower point: that the creed is genuinely early — on that, believers and atheists alike agree. What is contested is an Aramaic original, and a dedicated study of the formula partly dissents on a specifically Aramaic or Jerusalem origin and on the very earliest dating.
honestState.fairness: The broader survey figure on the resurrection data should be cited carefully: it is Gary Habermas’s own running compilation of the published literature, not a randomized poll of scholars, and critics have questioned how the sample was assembled. And James D. G. Dunn’s “formulated as tradition within months of Jesus’ death” is the confident outer edge of the few-years window on which the field broadly agrees, not a lone claim beyond it.
honestState.verdict: The creed establishes, with a confidence rare in the study of antiquity, that within a few years of the crucifixion the earliest Christians — including named men who claimed to have seen the risen Jesus — were already confessing his death, burial, resurrection, and appearances. It forecloses the easy theory that the resurrection was a legend grown ripe over generations. It does not, on its own, prove that Jesus rose; it proves that the belief is early and the witnesses sincere, and it hands the deeper question — what best explains their experiences and the empty tomb — to the wider argument. And this is what we hold to be true: Jesus of Nazareth was bodily raised from the dead, as this creed confesses, and the wider case — the empty tomb, the failure of the alternatives, the conversions of James and Paul — shows it.

order: Paul transmits a formula he received — a creed older than his letter.
Tracing the chain through Paul’s biography dates its content within roughly two to five years of the crucifixion.
Therefore the resurrection proclamation is earliest-stratum testimony, not accumulated legend.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and what it does NOT rest on.
cards.a: Paul transmits a formula he says he received — a creed older than his letter. It rests on the cumulative weight of the receiving/delivering language, the non-Pauline diction, and the creedal structure; it does not stand or fall on the contested Aramaic question.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and the step that makes the date a floor, not a guess.
cards.a: Tracing the chain through Paul’s conversion and his Jerusalem visit three years later dates the creed’s content within roughly two to five years of the crucifixion. The step: whenever Paul received it, the tradition itself must predate his receipt of it.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and not reach?
cards.a: That the resurrection proclamation — died, buried, raised, appeared, with named witnesses — is earliest-stratum testimony, not accumulated legend. It establishes early, sincere, eyewitness-anchored belief; that the belief was true is a further inference, argued on separate grounds.

cards.q: Why does the pair “delivered … received” matter?
cards.a: It is the precise idiom used in Judaism for the transmission of authoritative tradition. Paul is not narrating his own experience here; he is handing on something handed to him.

cards.q: What does the creed’s vocabulary show — and what is the limit on the Aramaic name for Peter?
cards.a: “For our sins,” “he has been raised” in a particular perfect form, “the twelve,” and “according to the Scriptures” cluster non-Pauline vocabulary into a few lines. Limit: Paul himself usually calls him Cephas, so the name points to a Semitic-speaking milieu rather than proving non-Pauline wording.

cards.q: Why does the shape of the lines count as evidence?
cards.a: Balanced clauses, each introduced by hoti (“that”), in a fourfold rhythm — died, was buried, was raised, appeared — read as a confession to be memorized rather than prose to be composed on the fly.

cards.q: Why does Paul’s fifteen-day visit to Jerusalem matter to the date?
cards.a: The verb Paul uses connotes inquiry — getting to know a person and, plausibly, his account — and the two men he names there are precisely two of the named recipients of appearances in the creed. Whether he received the formula at his conversion or had it confirmed in that fortnight, it predates his receipt of it.

cards.q: The external anchor for Paul’s chronology — what does it fix, and what does it not?
cards.a: It fixes a Roman proconsul’s term in Achaia, and via Paul’s appearance before his tribunal at Corinth it anchors Paul’s stay there; the earlier stages of his career are reckoned backward from that fixed point. It dates the proconsul, and so anchors Paul; it does not by itself date the creed.

cards.q: Reply to: the creed says Jesus appeared “to the twelve,” but only eleven were left.
cards.a: A category mistake: “the Twelve” is not a running head-count but the fixed name of the apostolic body, used even where it cannot mean twelve people; the Gospels say “the eleven” precisely when eleven is meant. A deliberate institutional label, not a slip of the tally — the mainstream reading, though a determined skeptic may still call the title idealized.

cards.q: If Paul added vv. 6-7 himself, what does the early-dating argument lose?
cards.a: Little: it leans on Cephas, a recipient who sits inside the four-line core (v. 5), not on the appended roll. That core carries the received/delivered formula, the non-Pauline diction, and the liturgical rhythm. A composite text with an early core is still an early core — and the early core is all the argument needs.

cards.q: Why is the five-hundred report, found only in Paul, not a weakness?
cards.a: The five hundred are reported only by Paul, not in the Gospels; but Paul’s closeness to the tradition — he had met its named witnesses — is precisely the point, not a weakness. And the early-dating argument never leaned on them.

cards.q: How secure is the early date — and what is its confident outer edge?
cards.a: About as close to a consensus as ancient history offers: believers and atheists alike agree the creed is genuinely early, and even an atheist New Testament scholar who denies the resurrection dates its elements “to the first two years after the crucifixion of Jesus... not later than three years.” “Within months” is the confident outer edge of the few-years window the field broadly agrees on, not a lone claim beyond it.

obj.q: The resurrection is a legend. It grew by accretion over decades, the original facts blurred by time and distance until a dying-and-rising god emerged.
obj.model: The creed cuts against that. Paul quotes a fixed formula he says he received, marked by the received/delivered language, the non-Pauline diction, and the liturgical rhythm, and counting back through Paul’s biography places its origin within roughly two to five years of the crucifixion — recited by the very people (Peter, James, “the twelve”) who claimed to be its witnesses. The window is too narrow for legendary embellishment to have done its slow work, and the named, living witnesses functioned as a check. That does not, by itself, prove the resurrection: it proves the belief is early and the witnesses sincere, and hands the deeper question — what best explains their experiences — to the wider argument.

obj.q: Grant the early date. It was visions, and nothing else — perhaps as few as a handful of followers had visionary experiences akin to “bereavement visions,” and these were retold and embellished until the tradition spoke of mass appearances.
obj.model: Grant what is true in it: bereavement visions are real and common, and the bare words “they saw him,” taken alone, do not by themselves rule out a vision. But hallucinations are, as a rule, private and individual; the creed reports a group appearance — “then to the twelve” sits inside the four-line core (v. 5), recited within a few years of the cross, and the window is too narrow for legendary embellishment to have done its slow work. A collective hallucination of the kind needed here — many people independently converging on the same seen-and-heard risen Jesus — has no established clinical basis. The hypothesis must also account for James, a skeptic during Jesus’ ministry, and Paul, an active persecutor with no grief-driven longing to see Jesus restored — neither fits the bereavement profile — and it must explain the empty tomb, which many scholars publishing on the question accept as historical (though it is more contested than the appearances), and which a purely visionary belief leaves unaddressed. That is precisely where it fails as the best explanation of the full set of facts.

obj.q: It isn’t one creed, it’s a patchwork: Paul enlarged a received core with material of his own. And it can’t even count — it says “the twelve” when Judas was dead and only eleven were left.
obj.model: First, the “inconsistency” is a category mistake. “The Twelve” is not a running head-count; it is the fixed name of the apostolic body — John calls Thomas “one of the Twelve” (John 20:24) when Judas is already gone, and Matthew and Luke say “the eleven” precisely when eleven is meant. Second, and decisively, conceding that Paul may have expanded the list beyond the core costs the early-dating argument little, because that argument leans on Cephas, a recipient who sits inside the four-line core (v. 5), not on the appended roll. That core carries the received/delivered formula, the non-Pauline diction, and the liturgical rhythm. A composite text with an early core is still an early core — and the early core is all the argument needs.

obj.q: The experiences were real and early — but psychological. Peter’s vision came from guilt over his denial; Paul’s resolved a repressed inner conflict.
obj.model: The reconstruction smuggles in a speculative psychoanalysis of figures we cannot put on the couch; the “guilt complex” and “Christ complex” it posits are read into the texts rather than out of them. The honest concession is that this reading is right about the date and right that the disciples had experiences they took to be appearances; the dispute is entirely over their cause, and there the psychological mechanism is conjecture, not evidence. And, like the bereavement reading, it leaves the group appearances, the conversion of James, and the empty tomb unexplained.

unseen.q: Fine, the creed is early. But its “appearances” were revelatory visions of a celestial being who was never on earth. The verb “appeared” (ōphthē) is the language of revelation, and the creed mentions no one seeing Jesus before his death.
unseen.model: Answer it on the texts, not with a label — and it is the texts that defeat it. The same Paul who recites the creed names Jesus’ brother James as a man he met — “James the Lord’s brother” (Galatians 1:19) — and speaks of Jesus as “born of woman, born under the law” (Galatians 4:4). A flesh-and-blood brother whom Paul personally met, and a birth from a woman under the law, are exactly what a celestial-only Jesus cannot accommodate. Nor can “brother” be the generic title for any believer: Paul lists “the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas” (1 Corinthians 9:5), setting the Lord’s brothers apart as a distinct group. As for ōphthē: it is indeed the standard Septuagint verb for divine appearances, but it is also used of ordinary appearing (Acts 7:26, of Moses appearing to two quarreling Israelites), and Paul marks his own experience as the exception rather than the pattern — “last of all, as to one untimely born” (15:8), closing the list rather than typifying it.
